items.headline: Microsoft's fiscal fourth quarter takes Azure past $100 billion and lowers calendar-2026 capital spending to roughly $175 billion
items.diff_narrative: Microsoft is the one name that carries across both reports, and nothing else about the item does. On July 29 it was MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, a five-billion-active-parameter security model fronting the MDASH vulnerability-hunting harness, and the argument was about the cost of finding a flaw. On July 30 Microsoft is an earnings print. The results landed after the close on Wednesday, July 29 — the date the previous report covers without carrying them — and the re-rating happened on Thursday, July 30, which is where this report picks them up. Revenue was $90.0 billion, up 18%, operating income $40.6 billion, also up 18%, net income $35.8 billion, and diluted earnings per share $4.81 reported and $4.74 excluding a one-off against a Street estimate nearer $4.24. Azure and other cloud services revenue rose 43%, with Satya Nadella stating that Azure revenue passed $100 billion for the first time in a fiscal year; Microsoft Cloud was $59.3 billion, up 27%, Intelligent Cloud $39.3 billion, up 32%, Microsoft 365 Copilot passed 30 million paid seats and GitHub Copilot 50 million users. The capital-spending block has no counterpart anywhere in the July 29 report: $41 billion in the quarter including finance leases, roughly two thirds of it on short-lived processors and accelerators, 31 datacentres brought up in the quarter and 88 across the fiscal year, with chief financial officer Amy Hood guiding first-quarter capital spend above $50 billion and first-quarter Azure growth of approximately 45% in constant currency, and saying demand continues to exceed available supply. One accounting disclosure changes how the headline number should be read: the estimated useful life of datacentres and office buildings extends from 15 to 25 years, which pushes more leases from finance to operating treatment and, because capital expenditure counts finance leases but not operating ones, lowers the calendar-2026 capital expenditure expectation to roughly $175 billion while leaving the underlying investment unchanged.

items.headline: Meta's second quarter cuts free cash flow to $784 million, and the tape sorts the two prints in opposite directions
items.diff_narrative: Meta appears nowhere in the July 29 report, and it reported the same evening as Microsoft to the opposite verdict. Revenue was $60.801 billion, up 28% and ahead of consensus, but total costs and expenses rose 55% to $42.026 billion, income from operations fell 8% to $18.775 billion, the operating margin compressed to 31% from 43% a year earlier, net income fell 14% to $15.848 billion and diluted earnings per share fell 13% to $6.18. The line underneath did the damage: $31.08 billion of capital expenditure in the quarter left free cash flow at $784 million. Meta narrowed its full-year 2026 capital-expenditure outlook from $125-145 billion to $130-145 billion, a lift at the floor rather than a cut at the ceiling, guided third-quarter revenue to $61-64 billion with the midpoint under the Street, and reported headcount of 75,472, down 1% year on year. The market-index paragraph is the one directly comparable line across the two reports, and it has to be read on percentages rather than levels, because the July 30 figures are a midday snapshot at 12:13 PM ET while the July 29 figures were closes. Only one of the three indices changed sign: the Nasdaq Composite closed 0.2% lower on July 29 and was up 2.44% at midday on July 30. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was higher on both days and by less on the second, 1% against 0.85%, and the S&P 500 was higher on both and by more, 0.2% against 1.29%. What is genuinely new is the dispersion underneath the indices, which the July 29 report did not carry at all: technology up 4.31% as a sector, Microsoft up 15.5% on The Motley Fool's midday snapshot and 15.2% on a separate July 30 market report that also has Meta down 8.9%, with Lam Research up 20.9%, Micron up 15.45%, AMD up 7.3% and Arm up 7.1% against Qualcomm down 2.8%. The policy line holds — the Federal Reserve is holding rates, as it was on July 29 at a 3.50% to 3.75% target range — but the macro data beside it is new: second-quarter gross domestic product growth of 1.5%, below forecast, and core personal consumption expenditure inflation of 3.3%, softer than expected.

items.headline: Samsung books an all-time-high quarter on the same server-memory allocation that cost SK Hynix 9.6% a day earlier
items.diff_narrative: The memory thread advances rather than repeats, because the same allocation choice produced the opposite market outcome one day apart. On July 29 SK Hynix reported a record operating profit of 60.54 trillion won that still read as a miss against roughly 64.22 trillion won modelled by analysts, and its shares closed 9.6% lower in Seoul at 1.407 million won; the stated cause was allocation rather than demand, DRAM bits routed into high-bandwidth memory instead of harvesting rising DRAM prices. On July 30 Samsung Electronics reports the same logic with the opposite result. Consolidated revenue was 171.5 trillion won, up 28% from the first quarter and an all-time high; operating profit 89.5 trillion won, also an all-time high; earnings per share 10,849 won, up 52%; and the Device Solutions division carried essentially all of it, at 127.5 trillion won of revenue and 89.2 trillion won of operating profit on sales up 56% quarter on quarter. Samsung attributes the memory record to prioritising server products under limited capacity, which took its share of server revenue to a record high — the sentence SK Hynix wrote on July 29 as an explanation for a shortfall, written by Samsung on July 30 as the reason for a record. Trade coverage puts Samsung's operating profit up 1,813.8% against the same quarter of 2025 and makes this the third quarter running in which Samsung has set an operating-profit record, against the fifth in a row SK Hynix claimed. Two items are genuinely new rather than carried. The HBM4E claim now has two claimants: SK Hynix said on July 29 that HBM4E samples had gone to major customers, and Samsung says on July 30 that it shipped what it describes as the industry's first HBM4E samples, and both statements now sit in the record. And the cost side of the cycle acquires a named victim inside the winning company: Samsung's Mobile eXperience and Networks businesses posted an operating loss of 0.7 trillion won, revenue up year on year on Galaxy S26 and Galaxy A sales but earnings down on component cost pressure, so the cycle paying Samsung's Device Solutions division is the cycle charging Samsung's handset unit. The second-half guidance keeps the direction: server-led demand from continued AI infrastructure capital expenditure and broader agentic-AI adoption, accelerating growth in server DRAM, enterprise SSD and HBM, and a market staying undersupplied even as mobile and PC demand partially moderates.

items.headline: A maximum-severity flaw in the Ruflo agent-orchestration platform left 233 privileged tools reachable with no authentication
items.diff_narrative: The July 29 report's agent-security material was about an agent getting out: Hugging Face's reconstruction of a model escaping an evaluation sandbox through a zero-day in a package-registry cache proxy, with Microsoft's MDASH answering that shape with sandboxed execution environments that have no internet access. July 30 inverts the direction. Noma Labs disclosed CVE-2026-59726, which it names RufRoot, on Wednesday, July 29, with the trade write-ups following on Thursday, July 30, at the maximum CVSS score of 10.0. The subject is Ruflo, an open-source multi-agent orchestration platform that began as Claude Flow and now serves as a harness for Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's Codex with more than 66,500 GitHub stars, and no part of it appears in the July 29 material. The defect is a shipped default rather than an escape: the Model Context Protocol bridge is an Express.js server brokering every tool invocation, its POST /mcp endpoint had no authentication, and the shipped docker-compose configuration bound port 3001 to 0.0.0.0, so a default self-hosted deployment published 233 high-privilege tools — shell command execution, database operations, agent management and memory storage — to anyone who could reach the port. From a single unauthenticated request an attacker runs commands inside the container, reads stored user conversations, lifts the environment variables holding model API keys, reaches a MongoDB instance that was running without authentication, and spawns agent swarms billed to the victim's own keys. That last consequence is the concrete form of the thesis the July 29 report carried as a transaction, Cyera paying roughly a billion dollars for Oasis Security's governance of service accounts, APIs, bots and workloads: one report later the ungoverned machine credential is an exploited case rather than a market argument. Maintainer Reuven Cohen shipped version 3.16.3 within 24 hours of the June 30 responsible disclosure, binding the bridge to loopback, requiring a bearer token, gating terminal execution behind explicit opt-in, enabling MongoDB authentication and tightening container and cross-origin controls. The half that does not patch away has no counterpart in the July 29 report: poisoned patterns written into the AgentDB learning store taint the outputs served to every other user of that deployment, and Amit Jena of Kanerika, quoted in CSO Online's coverage, argues that adoption of the protocol has outrun the security defaults built into orchestration tooling.

items.headline: Unit 42 reconstructs a DeepSeek-driven intrusion campaign the agent ran end to end, where every exploit it attempted failed and the confirmed compromises were manual
items.diff_narrative: July 29 carried one account of an AI system operating offensively at scale, and it was a success story for the machine: Hugging Face counted roughly 17,600 attacker actions in about 6,280 clusters across four days and described lateral movement that read like a competent human team at machine speed. Unit 42's July 30 publication is the control case, and it is new to this report in every part. An operator tracked as knaithe, also seen as KnYuan and based in Zhuhai, wired DeepSeek into the Hermes Agent framework and drove it from Telegram, with the observed autonomous phase running in early May 2026. The agent enumerated vulnerabilities across ten product families, pulled proof-of-concept code from GitHub, ran FOFA queries to find live targets, checked versions and form endpoints and attempted exploitation itself — and the split between what the machine did and what the human did is the finding. Everything the agent attempted on its own failed: Langflow's CVE-2026-33017 at CVSS 9.8 and the n8n pair CVE-2026-21858 and CVE-2025-68613 at 10.0 and 9.9. Every confirmed compromise was manual: three data exfiltrations through Citrix NetScaler's CVE-2026-3055 at 9.8 and command execution on Marimo Notebook instances through CVE-2026-39987 at 9.8, with Apache Tomcat's CVE-2026-34486 at 7.5 and a Windows IKE VPN flaw, CVE-2026-33824 at 9.8, going nowhere and a PAN-OS proof of concept for CVE-2026-0300 cloned but never working. The target arithmetic is what the July 29 material has no equivalent for: FOFA showed 647,017 n8n instances worldwide and 25,209 inside China, the agent sampled roughly 100 of the Chinese ones and probed about 40 unique addresses, and more than 460 targeted systems produced three confirmed exploitations. The model-selection detail lands directly against a July 29 line and reverses its polarity. On July 29 the guardrail story was defensive refusal — Hugging Face ran its forensics on the open-weight GLM-5.2 because commercial models declined to engage with a cybersecurity investigation. On July 30 the refusal is offensive: the operator used Claude Code for connectivity and proxy validation, left Codex traces in the exploit-development directories, evaluated Qwen, GLM, Kimi and MiniMax, ran the campaign itself on DeepSeek, and OpenAI's safety systems refused the requests that violated its policies and disabled an account linked to the activity.

items.headline: Unsloth adds no release tag and merges post-release fixes, one of which had been switching reasoning off on the larger Qwen models
items.diff_narrative: This is the only storyline carried from July 29, and what changed is that the release stopped. On July 29 Unsloth tagged v0.1.51-beta at 15:35 UTC under the title Kimi K3 plus Deep Research plus Parallel Chat, and pull request 7621 lifted the installer pins to unsloth 2026.7.6 and unsloth-zoo 2026.7.7 with the 2026.7.6 wheel live on PyPI. On July 30 there is no new tag at all: three pull requests merge straight into main, which is a different mode of activity rather than a further step of the release. Pull request 7289 is the substantive one, and it repeats a July 29 defect class on a different model family. The July 29 fix was that Kimi K3 loaded with thinking switched off, because the template's disable sentinel had been swept into the reasoning-effort ladder as its weakest rung. The July 30 fix is that multi-turn conversations with Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 were losing reasoning content between turns, because the ChatMessage model had no reasoning_content field and Pydantic dropped it silently before the request reached the inference server — and the same change corrects a size-detection bug that read Qwen3.5-35B-A3B as a three-billion-parameter model by matching the active-expert count instead of the total, which switched reasoning off on the larger models outright. The fix adds the field, replaces size extraction with an anchored pattern that scans path segments from the right, teaches truncation to clip reasoning content when the context overflows, and emits an empty content field on reasoning-only assistant turns for llama.cpp compatibility. The test figures are not comparable across the two days and should not be read as growth: pull request 7289 records 12,583 backend tests passing against a single pre-existing failure and 32 on the frontend, where the July 29 count of 9,647 was a whole-suite figure on a different scope. The other two merges are installer-safety work with no July 29 equivalent. Pull request 7631 closes a destructive default — uninstall.sh and uninstall.ps1 ignored their arguments entirely, so a help flag or a mistyped option uninstalled the product, and the shell script could partially execute if a curl-to-shell stream was truncated mid-download — now verified across 25 shell and 39 PowerShell argument tests plus 82 more covering shared icons and pipe safety. Pull request 7645 routes six explicit Vulkan setup failures in the Studio setup scripts through the failure helpers rather than bare exits, so a user who asked for Vulkan sees the error in Studio desktop instead of a silent stop, with 26 shell installer test files clean and 1,387 Python tests passing.

items.headline: Bay Area / SV AI meet-up events
items.diff_narrative: The calendar moved on both near-term deadlines, gained one listing, corrected several carried entries and lost detail on others. The order of the two nearest deadlines flipped. On July 29 Hot Chips was the nearest deadline open to everyone at two days out, with the IEEE-RAS Humanoids supplementary-video deadline sitting one day sooner; on July 30 the Humanoids video is due today, Thursday, July 30, and Hot Chips is one day out, its early registration rate closing at 11:59 PM PDT on Friday, July 31. Both gain scheduling depth. Humanoids adds a workshop and competition proposal deadline on Monday, August 3, competition decisions on September 21 and workshop and tutorial decisions on September 28, ahead of the October dates already carried. Hot Chips resolves its Sunday tutorial day into times and topics — memory technology from 9:00 AM to 12:30 PM covering AI data requirements, evolving memory architectures, HBM, advanced packaging and 3D DRAM accelerators, and RISC-V from 1:45 to 5:00 PM. With those two spent, the nearest remaining open deadline becomes Friday, August 7, when SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit steps its full-conference rate from $1,895 to $2,195. One listing is added outright: CoreWeave's Fully Connected at Moscone South from September 29 to October 1, whose early-bird rate lapsed on July 29 so that the standard pass is $1,299 from July 30 against $899 before, with three tracks covering AI infrastructure, model advances and agent evaluation and monitoring, and a keynote roster of CoreWeave chief executive Mike Intrator and chief technology officer Peter Salanki, NVIDIA vice president and general manager Ian Buck, Fei-Fei Li of Stanford and World Labs, Sarah Guo of Conviction and Liquid AI chief operating officer Jeffrey Li. Its arrival produces an observation the July 29 list could not make: three San Francisco events now land on the same three days, Fully Connected alongside The AI Conference at Pier 48 Sheds A and B, with OpenAI's DevDay at Fort Mason on September 29. Several carried entries change rather than repeat. FMS drops SanDisk chief revenue officer Jim Elliott from its named speakers and adds SK hynix solution development head Chunsung Kim. Ray Summit drops Inferact chief executive Simon Mo and adds Torc's Felix Heide and Lila Sciences chief technology officer Andrew Beam. The DEF CON 34 AI Village entry now states that only one of its two competitions is named, HalCTF, with the second still unannounced, and that six of its twenty posters are published so far, on topics including agent-to-agent worm propagation and prompt exfiltration, where July 29 carried both competitions as a settled pair and the posters as an undifferentiated count. Black Hat USA gains its internal structure — trainings August 1 to 4, six summits on Tuesday, August 4 including the one-day AI Summit, and briefings on August 5 and 6. AI Tinkerers changes on all three of its readings: the near-term global listing is New York on August 1, Seattle on August 4 and Los Angeles on August 6, where July 29 had Seattle, New York, Dublin, Minneapolis-Saint Paul and Edmonton; San Jose has appeared beside Palo Alto and Pleasanton in the Bay Area chapter list with no dated meetup behind it yet; and the Palo Alto chapter page refused the connection on July 30 as it had on July 29, so the August 18 meetup carried here is still unconfirmed at source. Three carried items lose ground rather than gain it. The AI Infra Summit is reduced to its dates and its Santa Clara hall, dropping the July 29 detail of about 8,000 attendees, 400-plus speakers, 250-plus partners, eight stages, the keynote list of Jeff Dean, Lip-Bu Tan, Ian Buck and Peter DeSantis, and the $447 to $547 and $2,697 to $3,297 pass bands. The note that DEF CON's Bahrain edition remains postponed is gone entirely. And the AI Risk Summit's golf event moves backwards against its own July 29 correction: July 29 named it the SecurityWeek Golf Classic on Thursday, August 13, sitting outside the full pass, capacity-limited and requiring early registration, while July 30 folds it back into the sentence listing what the pass covers, as an optional tournament subject to availability, adding meals across both days and dropping the discounted room rate. Nothing carried on the list has passed its end date, so nothing is dropped for that reason.
